warmup.q: The balance program keeps each account's balance in files on its computer's own disk, and also writes every new balance to a second log in Kafka. The computer breaks, and the program starts again on another computer whose disk is empty. What does it do before it handles the next payment?
options: Starts every balance at zero: the balances on the old disk are gone for good
Reads every payment again, from the very first one
Reads back the log of new balances into fresh files, then carries on from the last payment it had saved as done
Copies the files from another running copy of the program over the network
warmup.why: Every change to the balances also went to that second log, which Kafka keeps, so the new computer replays it into fresh files and then carries on with the payments from where the program last saved its place. Reading every payment again from the first one would take hours, and fails once Kafka has deleted its oldest payments. Another copy of the program can answer questions about its own balances, but a rebuild never copies from it. The second section takes this apart.

sections.h: A balance is the payments log added up into a table
sections.html:
Let's build the balance program from the opening. The payments app writes every card payment to a Kafka topic called payments. A topic is a named log in Kafka: programs add records to its end and read them in order. Each record has a key, the value it's filed under, and here the key is the account: acct-17 paid 30.00, acct-17 got 5.00 back. Kafka splits a topic into partitions, separate logs that can be read side by side. Every record with the same key goes to the same partition (Producers I: keys, partitions and ordering). A record's position in its partition is called its offset.

The program must answer "what is acct-17's balance right now?" for 2 million accounts, while about 3,000 payments a second arrive. These numbers are made up, but they're the size of a real payments company.

The first version is a plain consumer, a program that reads a topic in a loop, as in Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees. It keeps a map in memory, a HashMap<String, Long> from account to balance, and adds each payment to the account's entry. Reads are instant. That works until the first restart. Then the map is empty, and the only way back is to read payments again from the oldest record. Seven days at 3,000 a second is 1.8 billion records, and at 100,000 records a second the replay takes five hours. Worse, Kafka deletes records older than a set time, the retention period (Partitions and segments on disk: retention and compaction), so the rebuilt map would be wrong anyway.

The second version keeps the balances in a database, one update per payment. A restart now costs nothing. But every payment waits about 1 ms for the trip to the database and back. And the update and the consumer's note of how far it has read are two separate writes. A crash between them counts a payment twice or not at all, the problem that Transactions and exactly-once started from.

The third version keeps the map next to the code. Each time an entry changes, it also appends the new value to a Kafka topic of its own. After a restart, it reads back that topic instead of the payments. The topic only needs the latest value per account. Log compaction, Kafka's way of deleting old records that have a newer one with the same key, keeps exactly that. So a restart reads about 2 million records, not 1.8 billion. That's the café owner who also writes each new total, "Sam owes 12.50", as a line in a notebook kept in the office safe. If the box of cards is lost, she rebuilds it from the notebook.

Kafka Streams is that third version as a library: code you add to your own program, not a separate program to run. It reads input topics, runs your processing and writes output topics, in a loop it runs for you. It keeps the map, which it calls state, and logs every change of it to Kafka. You describe the processing as a topology: a graph of steps from input topics to output topics.

Two types carry the model. A KStream is a stream of events: each record is something that happened, so two records with the same key are two events. A KTable is a table: each record is the new value for its key and replaces the one before. You get a table from a stream by folding it: start each account at 0, then add every payment in turn. You get a stream back from a table by listing its changes, one record per update. The log: Kafka's one big idea called this the stream-table duality. A table is a log folded down to the latest value per key, and a table's history is a log again.

Here's the balance program in Java, then in Kotlin:

Java
StreamsBuilder builder = new StreamsBuilder();
KTable<String, Long> balances = builder
        .stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()))   // KStream: one record per payment
        .groupByKey()                                                        // already keyed by account
        .aggregate(() -> 0L, (account, amount, balance) -> balance + amount, // the fold: start at 0, add
                Materialized.<String, Long, KeyValueStore<Bytes, byte[]>>as("balances")
                        .withKeySerde(Serdes.String()).withValueSerde(Serdes.Long()));
balances.toStream()                                                          // KTable -> its changes
        .to("balances", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()));
Topology topology = builder.build();
Kotlin
val builder = StreamsBuilder()
val balances: KTable<String, Long> = builder
    .stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()))      // KStream: one record per payment
    .groupByKey()                                                           // already keyed by account
    .aggregate({ 0L }, { _, amount, balance -> balance + amount },          // the fold: start at 0, add
        Materialized.`as`<String, Long, KeyValueStore<Bytes, ByteArray>>("balances")
            .withKeySerde(Serdes.String()).withValueSerde(Serdes.Long()))
balances.toStream()                                                         // KTable -> its changes
    .to("balances", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()))
val topology = builder.build()

groupByKey collects the records of each key, aggregate folds them into a table named balances, and toStream turns the table's changes back into records for the balances topic. The Serdes tell Kafka how to turn keys and values into bytes and back: the keys are strings, and the amounts are whole cents in a Long. The Kotlin version makes the same four calls. It puts as in backticks, because as is a Kotlin keyword, and passes plain lambdas where Java writes () -> 0L.

The Try it runs this topology in TopologyTestDriver, a test tool that pushes records through a topology with no Kafka running at all. That leaves one question: where does the balances table live?

The topology has four steps, which Kafka Streams calls nodes: read payments, add up into the store balances, turn the table's changes into a stream, and write balances. sections.h: The table lives on local disk, and a changelog topic backs it up
sections.html:
Where is the balances table? On the disk of the computer that runs the program. Kafka Streams keeps it in a state store, which is RocksDB unless you choose otherwise. RocksDB is a key-value database, one that stores a value under each key and finds it by key, like our map. It runs as a library inside your program and keeps its data in files on the local disk, under the folder set by state.dir. The Try it prints the path, build/streams-state/balance-<run>/0_0/rocksdb/balances. A read or a write is a local call that takes microseconds (millionths of a second), with no trip over the network.

The 0_0 in that path is a task. Kafka Streams splits the work into tasks, one per input partition: with 6 partitions of payments, tasks 0_0 to 0_5. Each task owns its input partition, its slice of the store and the matching partition of the changelog (below). You can run several copies of the program, called instances, and they share out the tasks the way a consumer group shares out partitions (Consumer groups and rebalancing).

That only works because every record of one account sits in one partition, so one task sees them all. groupByKey keeps the key the payments app chose, so nothing moves. Group by anything else, say by shop, with groupBy((account, amount) -> merchantOf(account)), and each shop's records are spread over every partition. Kafka Streams then first writes every record to an internal topic whose name ends in -repartition, under the new key, and reads it back. That's an extra write and an extra read for every record.

A total can only be added up where all of a key's records meet. Key the input by the key you add up on.

Every write to the store also goes to the store's changelog topic, named <application.id>-<store>-changelog, which Kafka Streams creates with compaction on (cleanup.policy=compact). The application.id is the name you give the program, and it names everything the program owns: its consumer group, its internal topics and its local folder. The changelog is the café owner's notebook in the safe.

When an instance starts a task and the local store is missing, say because the program moved to a computer with an empty disk, it restores the store first. It reads the changelog partition from the beginning into a new RocksDB. Only then does it carry on with payments, from the last offset it committed: the position it last saved as done. In the Try it, the restore reads 1,000 records for 10 accounts. Kafka stores each partition as a series of files called segments, and compaction never touches the newest one, the active segment, which is still being written. This changelog is young, so all of it is still in that segment. The wait grows with the store: a 50 GB store read at 100 MB a second takes more than 8 minutes, and that partition's payments wait that long.

Two settings shorten the wait. num.standby.replicas=1 makes another instance keep a warm copy of each store by reading its changelog all the time, so after a failure only the last few records need replaying. That's a second café that keeps its own box of cards up to date from a copy of the notebook. The record cache, statestore.cache.max.bytes (10 MiB by default), merges updates to the same key between commits (every 30 seconds by default), so the changelog and the output get fewer records. The demos set it to 0 to show every update.

A KTable is split like its topic: each task holds only the rows of its own partition. Sometimes every task needs every row, say a small table of shop categories that each payment looks up, whatever its account. A GlobalKTable is the other choice. builder.globalTable("merchant-categories") gives every instance a full copy (the code calls shops merchants). The copy is read from all partitions of the topic, and loaded completely before the instance handles anything. It has no changelog of its own: to restore, it reads its source topic again. It costs a full copy per instance and a slower start, and the next lesson, Stream joins and complex event processing, shows the lookups it makes easy.

The café picture breaks at scale. The owner keeps one box, while each task keeps its own slice, and the program writes thousands of notebook lines a second. The stepper follows one task through four payments, a lost disk and a restore.

try.title: Lose the local store and get it back
steps: From the labs folder, start Kafka if it isn't running: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait. Docker runs programs in sealed boxes called containers, and this starts one Kafka computer, a broker, in one.

Run RestoreDemo (command below). Run 1 adds up 1,000 payments for 10 accounts into the store and stops cleanly. The demo then deletes the program's local state folder and starts run 2. It takes 20 to 40 seconds, most of it two Kafka Streams start-ups.
Predict: how many changelog records does run 2 restore, 10 (one per account) or more?

sections.h: Windows in Kafka Streams: stream time and a grace period
sections.html:
The company wants an alarm when an account has more than 3 debits, payments out of it, within one minute. A stolen card is often used several times in quick succession. That's a count per account per window of event time, which Time in streams built engine by engine. What's left is how Kafka Streams spells it.

Event time is each record's timestamp, which the producer, the program that writes the record to Kafka, sets when the payment happens. (A TimestampExtractor can read it from a field of the record instead.) The window kinds from the last lesson have these names. TimeWindows makes tumbling and hopping windows, lined up with the clock, each including its start and leaving out its end. SlidingWindows makes one window per record, ending at the record, with both ends included. SessionWindows makes sessions per key, ended by a quiet gap. Mind the names: Flink and the Dataflow model call a hopping window "sliding". The figure shows three of the kinds over the same debits.

There's no watermark object. Its place is taken by stream time: the largest timestamp a task has seen so far, which never goes back. A window stays open until stream time passes its end plus the grace period. A record for it after that is dropped, and counted in the dropped-records-total metric. In the last lesson's terms, the watermark is stream time minus the grace. With TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(1), Duration.ofSeconds(30)), the window from 10:00 to 10:01 takes records until stream time reaches 10:01:30. A longer grace keeps more late records, but every window stays in the store longer, and its final count comes later.

Stream time belongs to the task, not to the key. In the Try it, a debit of acct-3 moves stream time forward and closes acct-7's window. And a task that receives nothing has a stream time that doesn't move, so its last windows never close: the last lesson's watermark that runs too slow.

Here's the rule, in Java and then in Kotlin:

Java
builder.stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()))
        .filter((account, amount) -> amount < 0)                                      // debits only
        .groupByKey()
        .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(1), Duration.ofSeconds(30)))
        .count()                                                                      // KTable<Windowed<String>, Long>
        .toStream((window, count) -> window.key())                                    // the plain account id
        .filter((account, count) -> count > 3)                                        // more than 3 a minute
        .to("fraud-alerts", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()));
Kotlin
builder.stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()))
    .filter { _, amount -> amount < 0 }                                             // debits only
    .groupByKey()
    .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(1), Duration.ofSeconds(30)))
    .count()                                                                        // KTable<Windowed<String>, Long>
    .toStream { window, _ -> window.key() }                                         // the plain account id
    .filter { _, count -> count > 3 }                                               // more than 3 a minute
    .to("fraud-alerts", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()))

The windowed count is a table keyed by account and window, so it sends out (emits) an update for each debit: 1, 2, 3, 4. That's the last lesson's "answer early and correct later", with each new count replacing the one before for its window. The rule keeps counts above 3, so a fifth debit raises a second alarm. suppress(untilWindowCloses(...)) would emit one final count per window instead, but only after the grace period, which is too late to stop a card.

Windows also limit how long a join of two streams waits for a match, and tables are what other streams look things up in; the next lesson takes both apart. But this program counts money, so first we have to ask what a crash does to its counts.

sections.h: A crash can count a payment twice, and exactly-once fixes it
sections.html:
Picture the balance program with its default settings. Every 30 seconds (commit.interval.ms), it saves its stores and changelogs, then commits its input offsets: it tells Kafka how far it has read. Between commits, updates already reach the changelog: every one with the record cache off, and whatever the cache lets go of with it on. This is called at-least-once (Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees met it): after a crash, nothing is lost, but some records are handled twice.

Now let an instance die 20 seconds after a commit. The next owner of its task restores a store that already includes those 20 seconds of updates. Then it reads the same 20 seconds of payments again, from the committed offset, and adds every one of them a second time. Nothing logs an error, and the balances are wrong. Tests don't catch it either, because TopologyTestDriver never crashes.

processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 fixes it with the machinery of Transactions and exactly-once. A transaction is a group of writes that Kafka makes visible all together or not at all. Each stream thread, one of the program's paths of work, gets a producer that writes in transactions. One commit interval's output records, changelog writes and input offsets go into one transaction. A crash cancels, or aborts, the open transaction, and the restore reads only committed changelog records, so each payment counts once. The commit interval drops to 100 ms to keep transactions short. Programs that read balances need isolation.level=read_committed, so that they skip records from aborted transactions. The Try it shows the cost on the changelog: 1,000 updates plus 3 commit markers, small records that mark a transaction as done.

The guarantee covers what the program writes to Kafka, and nothing else. A call from inside the topology to a bank's computer, or an email sent from it, can still happen twice. Fault tolerance in stream processing: checkpoints and exactly-once compares this approach with Flink's. The defaults also expect at least 3 brokers, the computers that make up Kafka. The log that tracks transactions wants 3 copies, with at least 2 of them up to date, and the lab's single broker in kafka.yml lowers both numbers to 1.

At-least-once is fine for a chart and wrong for money. Turn on exactly_once_v2 for balances.

Two newer settings are worth knowing by name. The first decides who shares out the tasks. By default (group.protocol=classic), the instances work it out among themselves, with the rules from Consumer groups and rebalancing. With group.protocol=streams, from KIP-1071 (a numbered Kafka Improvement Proposal), Kafka's own brokers decide instead. It has been ready for real use since Kafka 4.2, for its core features. A running program can't switch to it without stopping every instance first, and a few features are still missing (Go deeper has the list).

The second decides what happens to a bad record. A payment whose bytes can't be turned back into a payment is a poison pill, in the words of Failure handling: poison pills, retries and dead letters. By default it stops the program: LogAndFailExceptionHandler throws an error, and the stream thread dies. Since Kafka 4.2 (KIP-1034), you can set errors.dead.letter.queue.topic.name. The built-in handlers then write the bad record's key and value to that topic, a dead letter queue. They add headers, labels on the record such as __streams.errors.exception and __streams.errors.offset, that say what went wrong and where. With LogAndContinueExceptionHandler as the handler for unreadable records, the program then carries on with the next one.

KIP-1034: Dead letter queue in Kafka Streams

opening:
Picture a café that lets its regulars pay at the end of the month. By the till sits a box of cards, one per regular, with the amount owed in pencil. It's fast: the owner finds a card and changes one number.

Now make that box a program. It keeps 2 million running balances in memory and adds each payment as it arrives from Kafka, 3,000 a second. One night the computer restarts, and every balance is gone. Getting them back means reading every payment again from the start, and that takes hours.

Keeping the numbers in memory is tempting because it's fast and it passes every test. Tests never restart halfway through.

In Time in streams, we cut payments into windows and kept a count for each one, but never asked where those counts live. In this lesson, we'll add up payments into a table with Kafka Streams, find where the table lives, delete its disk on purpose and get it back. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with 2 million balances in memory that vanished at the first restart. Kafka Streams keeps the table on the local disk, writes every change to a compacted changelog topic, and rebuilds the table from it when the disk is lost. With exactly_once_v2, a crash doesn't count a payment twice.

After you run RestoreDemo, open the folder labs/kafka/build/streams-state. Each run left a folder named after its application.id, with a folder per task and RocksDB's own files inside.

Next, we'll join a stream with another stream and with a table, and find out why the same join can give a different answer when you run it again.

compare.title: The balance topology in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: StreamsBuilder builder = new StreamsBuilder(); KTable<String, Long> balances = builder .stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())) // KStream: one record per payment .groupByKey() // already keyed by account .aggregate(() -> 0L, (account, amount, balance) -> balance + amount, // the fold: start at 0, add Materialized.<String, Long, KeyValueStore<Bytes, byte[]>>as("balances") .withKeySerde(Serdes.String()).withValueSerde(Serdes.Long())); balances.toStream() // KTable -> its changes .to("balances", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())); Topology topology = builder.build();

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: val builder = StreamsBuilder() val balances: KTable<String, Long> = builder .stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())) // KStream: one record per payment .groupByKey() // already keyed by account .aggregate({ 0L }, { _, amount, balance -> balance + amount }, // the fold: start at 0, add Materialized.`as`<String, Long, KeyValueStore<Bytes, ByteArray>>("balances") .withKeySerde(Serdes.String()).withValueSerde(Serdes.Long())) balances.toStream() // KTable -> its changes .to("balances", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())) val topology = builder.build()

compare.note: The same four calls. Java needs a type witness, the types written out in angle brackets in Materialized.<String, Long, KeyValueStore<Bytes, byte[]>>as(...), because the compiler can't work out the store's type from as("balances") alone. Kotlin writes Materialized.`as` in backticks, because as is a Kotlin keyword. It passes plain lambdas, short functions written in place, where Java expects its Initializer and Aggregator interfaces. In Kotlin, Long in a generic type is Java's java.lang.Long, so Serdes.Long() fits without a cast.

worked.title: Add each account's tier to its payments

steps.say: Read the tiers as a table. A tier is a label the company gives each account, such as gold for its best customers or watch for ones it keeps an eye on. account-tiers is a compacted topic keyed by account id, and each record is that account's current tier. builder.table turns it into a KTable with its own store.
steps.code: KTable<String, String> tiers = builder.table("account-tiers", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()));

alt.html: val tiers: KTable<String, String> = builder.table("account-tiers", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()))

steps.say: Join the payments stream with it. For each payment, Kafka Streams looks up the account's tier row as it is at that moment, and builds one output record from both. A later tier change doesn't touch payments already joined: a stream-table join is a lookup, not a window. The next lesson shows what this lookup gets wrong when a payment arrives late.
steps.code: builder.stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())) .join(tiers, (amount, tier) -> amount + " cents, tier " + tier) // the payment's key finds the row .to("payments-enriched", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()));

alt.html: builder.stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())) .join(tiers) { amount: Long, tier: String -> "$amount cents, tier $tier" } // the payment's key finds the row .to("payments-enriched", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()))

steps.say: Check that the two topics are co-partitioned before you run it: the same number of partitions, and the same rule for turning a key into a partition. Payment acct-17 must reach the task that holds acct-17's tier (Producers I: keys, partitions and ordering). Kafka Streams compares the partition counts when it starts, and refuses to run if they differ. It can't see which rule each producer used. A GlobalKTable of tiers would need neither.

Test it in TopologyTestDriver, and mind the order. A payment that arrives before its account's tier finds no row, and an inner join, which outputs only the records that found a match, drops it. With leftJoin it would come out with a null tier instead.
steps.code: payments.pipeInput("acct-1", 100L); // no tier yet: an inner join drops it tiers.pipeInput("acct-1", "gold"); payments.pipeInput("acct-1", 200L); assertThat(enriched.readKeyValuesToList()).containsExactly(KeyValue.pair("acct-1", "200 cents, tier gold"));

alt.html: payments.pipeInput("acct-1", 100L) // no tier yet: an inner join drops it tiers.pipeInput("acct-1", "gold") payments.pipeInput("acct-1", 200L) assertThat(enriched.readKeyValuesToList()).containsExactly(KeyValue("acct-1", "200 cents, tier gold"))

lab.title: Build a balance table and a windowed fraud rule
steps: From the labs folder, run the tests with the command above. All 13 fail. They need no Kafka: every test builds your topology and drives it with TopologyTestDriver, with the record cache off so that each update shows.

In BalanceTopology.kt, build the balance table: read PAYMENTS, group by the key it already has, aggregate from 0 into a store named STORE, and write every update to BALANCES. Also send the updates that leave a balance below zero to OVERDRAFTS. One test reads the changelog topic balance-app-balances-changelog, and another checks that the topology has no repartition topic.

In FraudRule.java, build the alarm rule: debits only, grouped by account, tumbling windows of window with grace, counted into STORE. For every count above limit, send an alert to ALERTS whose key is the plain account id and whose value is "<count> debits in <start>/<end>".
Run the tests until all 13 pass. The late-record tests replay the WindowDemo run: one late debit inside the grace period, and one after it.
hints: In Java, Materialized.<String, Long, WindowStore<Bytes, byte[]>>as(STORE) names a windowed store. In Kotlin, Materialized.`as`<String, Long, KeyValueStore<Bytes, ByteArray>>(STORE) names the balance store.
A windowed count's key is a Windowed<String>: w.key() is the account, and w.window().startTime() and endTime() are Instants whose toString() gives 2026-11-07T10:00:00Z.
If the late-record tests fail, check that you used TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(window, grace) and not ofSizeWithNoGrace.

drill.title: The fraud window from memory
drill.prompt: From memory, write a topology that counts debits per account in one-minute tumbling windows with 30 seconds of grace, and sends counts above 3 to fraud-alerts. Then answer: stream time is 10:01:25. Is a debit stamped 10:00:59 counted? And one stamped 10:00:10 that arrives when stream time is 10:01:31?

answer.html: builder.stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())) .filter((account, amount) -> amount < 0) // debits only .groupByKey() .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(1), Duration.ofSeconds(30))) .count() // KTable<Windowed<String>, Long> .toStream((window, count) -> window.key()) // the plain account id .filter((account, count) -> count > 3) // more than 3 a minute .to("fraud-alerts", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())); // 10:00:59 at stream time 10:01:25: counted. The window [10:00, 10:01) stays open until stream time // reaches 10:01:00 + 30 s = 10:01:30. // 10:00:10 at stream time 10:01:31: dropped, and counted in dropped-records-total. The window has closed.

The window [10:00, 10:01) stays open until stream time // reaches 10:01:00 + 30 s = 10:01:30. // 10:00:10 at stream time 10:01:31: dropped, and counted in dropped-records-total. The window has closed.

recap: Kafka Streams is a library inside your program that reads topics, runs your processing and writes topics, in a loop it runs for you. A KStream holds events, and a KTable holds the latest value per key. Adding up a stream makes a table, and a table's changes are a stream again.

A table lives in a local state store (RocksDB, in files under state.dir), split into tasks, one per input partition. Every write also goes to a compacted changelog topic, <application.id>-<store>-changelog. A GlobalKTable instead gives every instance a full copy of a small table.
A task that finds no local store rebuilds it from the changelog before it handles any record. The wait grows with the store, and standby replicas keep a warm copy ready.

The last lesson's windows are TimeWindows (tumbling and hopping), SlidingWindows and SessionWindows. Stream time, the largest timestamp a task has seen, minus the grace period plays the watermark: a window closes when stream time passes its end plus grace, and later records are dropped and counted.
With the default at-least-once, a crash between commits counts some payments twice. exactly_once_v2 puts the outputs, changelog writes and offsets of every 100 ms in one transaction.

The limits: exactly-once covers only what the program writes to Kafka, not the calls or emails it makes; a big store still takes minutes to restore; and TopologyTestDriver never crashes, so tests can't show the double count.

explain.prompt: A friend says: "Kafka Streams keeps its numbers in memory, so a crash loses them. Let's keep the balances in a database instead." Explain to them where the numbers really live, what happens after a crash or a lost disk, and what you would set for balances.
explain.answer: The numbers live in a RocksDB store on the local disk, one slice per task, and every write to it also goes to a compacted changelog topic in Kafka. After a crash, the next owner of the task, on the same computer or another one, rebuilds the store from that changelog before it handles anything. Then it carries on with the payments from the last committed offset. A lost disk costs time, not data. For a big store, a standby replica keeps a second copy up to date, so taking over takes seconds. For balances I'd set processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2, so that the changelog writes, the output and the input offsets commit together; with the default at-least-once, a crash can count some payments twice. Programs that read the output need read_committed, and Kafka needs three brokers for the log that tracks transactions. If the company's official record of balances is a database, it stays that. The Streams table is a fast copy that can always be rebuilt from the topics.

deeper.html:
Final results only. A windowed count sends out an update per record. suppress(Suppressed.untilWindowCloses(BufferConfig.unbounded())) holds them back and sends one record per window, once stream time passes its end plus grace. That's right for a daily total per shop, and wrong for a stolen-card alarm, which must fire on the fourth debit.

Sliding windows. SlidingWindows.ofTimeDifferenceAndGrace(...) makes a window around each record instead of on a fixed grid, so "more than 3 debits within any 60 seconds" catches 10:00:50 and 10:01:05 together, which tumbling windows split.

Interactive queries. streams.store(StoreQueryParameters.fromNameAndType("balances", QueryableStoreTypes.keyValueStore())) reads the local store, as RestoreDemo does. Each instance holds only its own tasks' keys. streams.queryMetadataForKey(...) tells you which instance holds a key, and you forward the question to it through a web endpoint of your own.

The streams rebalance protocol in detail. KIP-1071's group.protocol=streams was early access in Kafka 4.1, ready for its core features in 4.2, and got static membership in 4.4 (an instance that restarts quickly keeps its tasks). The brokers must have it turned on. It doesn't yet support topic subscriptions by pattern or warmup tasks. Standbys become a setting of the group, streams.num.standby.replicas, set with kafka-configs.sh, and the client's own num.standby.replicas is ignored.

Name your stores. Kafka 4.4 logs a warning when internal topics and stores have generated names, such as KSTREAM-AGGREGATE-STATE-STORE-0000000001. Adding one step to the topology can shift those numbers, and the program then looks for a changelog that doesn't exist. Name stores with Materialized.as, as the lab does, and steps with Named.as.

Tests that crash. TopologyTestDriver handles each record in turn and never crashes, so it can't show the at-least-once double count. To see it, run the program against a broker, kill it with kill -9 between commits, and compare the balances with and without exactly_once_v2.
